Abstract—The alternating current (AC) chance-constrained
optimal power flow (CC-OPF) problem addresses the economic
efficiency of electricity generation and delivery under generation
uncertainty. The latter is intrinsic to modern power grids because
of the high amount of renewables. Despite its academic success,
the AC CC-OPF problem is highly nonlinear and computationally
demanding, which limits its practical impact. For improving
the AC-OPF problem complexity/accuracy trade-off, the paper
proposes a fast data-driven setup that uses the sparse and hybrid
Gaussian processes (GP) framework to model the power flow
equations with input uncertainty. We advocate the efficiency of
the proposed approach by a numerical study over multiple IEEE
test cases that show up to two times speed-up and more accurate
solutions over state-of-the-art methods.
Index Terms—Power Flow, Chance-Constrained Optimization,
Gaussian processes, AC-OPF.
I. I NTRODUCTION
The increase in renewable energy generation is a primary
approach to reducing greenhouse emissions. Despite the eco-
nomic and ecological benefits of renewable energy sources
(RES), the uncertainty associated with RES generation, such
as wind and solar, leads to significant control challenges for
the Transmission System Operators (TSOs) [1]. Optimization
and feedback control algorithms should act on second and
sub-second levels to prevent the grid from impending energy
blackout due to RES uncertainty. Among such fundamental
tools, the optimal power flow (OPF) problem is key to finding
the economically optimal operation under security constraints.
Various methods address the accuracy and scalability of the
AC OPF problem under uncertainty, including seminal prob-
abilistic optimal power flow [2], and analytical and scenario-
based chance-constrained approaches [3], [4]. The chance-
constrained setup considered in this paper ensures that the
security constraints are satisfied with a high probability and
allows TSOs to balance operating costs and system security.
Unfortunately, Chance-Constrained (CC) AC-OPF with non-
linear Alternating Current-Power flow (AC-PF) equations are
known to be computationally demanding and often do not
have an analytical solution [3], [5], [6]. A simpler linear
version, chance-constraint direct current (DC) approximation
(DC CC-OPF) [4], [7], [8] has been widely studied in literature
and has a few scalable solutions [9], [10], but suffers from
conservative solutions. Furthermore, it requires knowledge of
the system parameters, such as line impedances without errors
and uncertainties.
The paper proposes to improve the AC CC-OPF scalability
using a data-driven method that builds upon the Gaussian
Process (GP) Regression framework to replace the power
flow equations using prior historical data. Note that GP-
based power-flow models have software implementations in
deterministic OPF formulations [11], and for CC-OPF in [12],
[13]. Compared to vanilla Gaussian process regression in [12],
however, our approach uses (1) a hybrid GP that combines
linear DC-PF with the data-driven estimation of the residuals
between DC-PF and AC-PF, and (2) uses sparse Gaussian
regression using few selective data for the estimation of the
hybrid GP. Both these steps significantly reduce our computa-
tional complexity without compromising the solution’s accu-
racy, making it amenable for real-time/online deployment. We
demonstrate the practical advantage of our approach against
state-of-the-art algorithms on multiple IEEE test cases.
This paper is organized as follows. Section II describes the
problem addressed and the uncertainty modeling. Section III
outlines the Gaussian Process Regression and its sparse ver-
sion. The hybrid approach to solve the AC CC-OPF problem is
given in Section IV. Section V presents numerical evaluation
results over various IEEE test cases. Section VI presents a
critical discussion, possible extensions, and a summary of the
paper.

This paper considers separable chance constraints, which

V. R ESULTS
We used an Intel Core i7-5500U CPU @ 2.40GHz with
8GB RAM for numerical computations and pandapower
[24] package to validate the results. The source code for
experiments is accessible online 1.
A. Case Study
Performance and scalability of the proposed hybrid sparse
GP CC-OPF method are evaluated over 9-bus and 39-bus IEEE
test cases. We assume the fluctuations in the system to be
15% of (forecasted) loads ( σl = 0 .15 pl) and 30% for the
renewable generations ( σrg = 0 .3 prg). Following [25], we
set the acceptable violation probabilities of generator limits to
ϵpg = 0.1% for controllable generators, and ϵy = 2.5% for all
other constraints.
1https://github.com/mile888/hybrid gp
B. Model Performance
The hybrid and full (no linear component) GPR models are
trained on residuals between datasets collected from full AC-
OPF and DC-OPF approximation. The synthetic data of the
IEEE 9-bus system consists of 8 input features and 15 outputs,
while for IEEE 39, the model has 37 inputs and 74 outputs. We
generated 75 and 200 random training samples for IEEE 9 and
39-bus systems and considered a different number of inducing
points of 10, 30, and 50 for both full and hybrid GPR models.
We use IPOPT [23] to solve both hybrid and full GP CC-
OPF and find a feasible solution with convergence tolerance
of ϵtol = 10−5.
The results in Table I indicate that the hybrid GPR model
with TA1 outperforms both RMSE and CPU time with respect
to the full GPR model with TA1 in [12]. Similarly, sparse ap-
proximation allows to significantly reduce the time complexity
for both hybrid and full approaches. In our experiments, we
notice that RMSE computed between the DC approximation
and the set of samples is RMSE = 6.65e−2 p.u. (IEEE 9)
and 3.04e−2 p.u. (IEEE 39). In other words, applying the
GPR model with a few samples leads to at least 6 times more
accurate approximation than the DC baseline.

C. Comparison of GP CC-OPF to Sample-Based Methods
In this section, we compare optimal objective function
value, computational time, and reliability of the proposed hy-
brid and full GP CC-OPF approaches with Scenario Approx-
imation (SA) CC-OPF [6]. In all cases, we use the first-order
Taylor approximation (TA1) as a function of linearization. The
empirical constraint violation is computed using 1000 Monte-
Carlo samples that follow (Gaussian) uncertainty distribution.
We compare our approach to two baselines. (A) Determin-
istic AC-OPF problem for each uncertainty realization and
taking a corresponding quantile in the output distribution. (B)
A deterministic AC-OPF for the mean load and RES, with
fixed and equal participation factor α∗. Notice that (A) is
unrealistic as it solves AC-OPF after uncertainty realization
(full-resource), while (B) does not optimize the participation
factor α. Thus (A) gives the upper (though unrealistic) bound
and (B) gives the lower bound on the feasible solution value.
Numerical evaluation of the bounds, given in Table II, shows
that the hybrid-sparse GP modeling provides a flexible scheme

E. Distributional Robustness
In operational practice, a joint distribution of renewables
and loads is not known exactly, and one needs to account for
it when solving a problem. Furthermore, distribution mismatch

is robust against a sufficiently large mismatch between the
expected distribution and the real one.

VI. C ONCLUSION
The paper studies various machine learning approaches to
chance-constrained AC optimal power flow problems. Because
of the high non-linearity of the problem, we focused mostly on
Gaussian Process Regression, one of the most popular model-
free approaches to approximate non-linear stochastic data.
As the Gaussian Process Regression has poor scalability, we
utilize a sparsity trick that allowed us to significantly reduce
the complexity. Finally, we proposed a hybrid GP approach
that uses a DC power flow approximation together with the
non-linear GP. This demonstrates higher robustness to missing
and corrupted data than the classical GP. Overall, this work’s
findings indicate that the hybrid sparse GP approach that we
proposed outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in terms
of both speed and accuracy for solving stochastic AC-OPF
problems.
